title: Active Galactic Nuclei
body:
An **active galactic nucleus** is a galaxy centre outshining the rest of the galaxy from a
region smaller than the solar system. Quasars are the most luminous and most distant examples.

The size limit is what forced the explanation. The output varies over days to months, and
nothing can vary faster than light crosses it, so the emitting region is light-days across
while producing more energy than a hundred billion stars.

The mechanism is accretion onto a supermassive [[Black Hole]]. Matter falling toward the
horizon forms a disc, friction inside the disc heats it to millions of degrees, and it radiates
across the spectrum. Accretion converts a far larger fraction of infalling mass into energy
than fusion does, which is what makes the output possible from so little material.

Quasars are almost all distant, which by the light-travel argument in
[[Astronomical Distance]] means almost all ancient. Active nuclei were common in the early
universe and are rare now, because the gas available to fall in has largely been used. The
[[Milky Way]]'s central black hole is quiet for that reason and would light up if given
something to eat.
